# JBS (JBS N.V.) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Easy to understand at the business-model level: JBS buys live cattle, hogs, and poultry, processes them into beef, pork, chicken, and prepared foods, and sells into grocery, foodservice, and export channels. No exotic technology or financial engineering. The complexity is elsewhere — in commodity-cycle timing, cross-border trade/export policy, and a controlling-family governance structure that a pure numbers read won't surface.

## Moat & Durability — Score 3/10
JBS is the largest protein processor in the world, with real diversification benefits: multiple species (beef/pork/poultry), multiple geographies (Brazil, US, Australia, Europe), and scale that smaller processors can't match on cost or distribution reach. That buys resilience — JBS is less likely than a single-plant regional player to be knocked out by one disease outbreak or one country's export ban. But it does not buy pricing power. Gross margin of 11.8% and operating margin of 3.07% are the signature of a commodity price-taker squeezed between volatile input costs (cattle, hogs, feed grain) and buyers (retailers, foodservice, export customers) who have their own negotiating leverage. This is a moat that helps JBS survive cycles better than peers, not one that lets it compound value independent of the cycle — hence a low score.

## Management & Capital Allocation
ROE of 13.4% sits on debt/equity of 283%, meaning leverage is the primary driver of the return, not operating efficiency; the packet gives no way to isolate an unlevered return on capital, and that leverage is itself a risk multiplier in a cyclical, thin-margin business. Beyond the numbers: JBS's controlling Batista family admitted to bribery of Brazilian officials in 2017 (part of the broader Car Wash-era corruption scandals), and the 2025 NYSE listing structure preserved family super-voting control in a way that drew objections from proxy advisors and some pension funds. None of that is in this packet's fields, but it is precisely the kind of governance signal Munger would weigh heavily and that a spreadsheet alone will never show — it argues for treating 'trustworthy management' as unproven at best.

## Predictability
Revenue growth of 13.8% is healthy on its face, but meatpacking margins move with cattle/hog/feed-grain cycles and disease events (avian flu, ASF) that are largely outside management's control, and a 3.07% operating margin leaves almost no cushion for a bad stretch. The forward P/E of 8.9x versus trailing 12.2x implies the market is pricing in a meaningful near-term earnings recovery — a bet on the cycle turning, not evidence of a steady compounder. This fails Munger's 'easy decision' test: predicting JBS's earnings three years out requires calling commodity cycles, not just reading a trend line.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Input-cost/margin compression**: a cattle, hog, or feed-grain price spike (or a weak export/demand environment) turns an already-thin ~3% operating margin negative, and there is very little buffer to absorb it.
2. **Leverage amplifies the cycle**: 283% debt/equity means a normal cyclical trough can become a refinancing or covenant crisis, particularly if credit markets tighten or rates stay elevated.
3. **Governance/regulatory shock**: given the Batista family's documented bribery history, ongoing antitrust/price-fixing exposure common across large meatpackers (chicken price-fixing litigation has touched the industry broadly), or a disease-driven export ban, any of these could hit revenue, trigger fines, or reopen questions about whether minority shareholders' interests are aligned with the controlling family's.

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($43.1B), trailing P/E (12.25x), forward P/E (8.89x), and FCF yield (1.9%) but not share count or share price directly. Using an approximate ~2.8B share count (a modeling assumption drawn from JBS's known post-2025-listing share structure, not sourced from this packet) implies a current price near $15.4/share, trailing EPS near $1.26/share, forward EPS near $1.73/share, and FCF/share near $0.29.

The earnings-yield/FCF-yield gap here is the central valuation problem: P/E of 12.2x implies an ~8.2% earnings yield, but FCF yield is only 1.9% — a much wider gap than a stable business should show, consistent with heavy ongoing capex and working-capital needs eating into reported profit. Rather than take reported EPS at face value or punish the business down to bare current-year FCF (which may be depressed by a growth-capex/working-capital year), I blend the two: averaging trailing and forward EPS (~$1.495/share) and haircutting ~25% for the demonstrated gap to cash generation gives normalized owner earnings of roughly **$1.10-$1.15/share**.

Applying a below-market multiple (9-11x) to reflect the thin moat, high leverage, and cyclicality:
- **Low case**: ~$9.50/share
- **High case**: ~$13.00/share

Midpoint ~$11.25/share vs. an implied current price of ~$15.4/share gives a margin of safety of roughly **-27%** — the stock is expensive relative to normalized owner earnings despite headline multiples (12.2x trailing, 8.9x forward, 6.68x EV/EBITDA) that read as statistically cheap. That disconnect is the tell: this looks cheap only if you take reported earnings at face value and ignore both the cash-conversion gap and the leverage load.

## The Cloning Caveat
Christopher Davis (Davis Advisors) has been building a position across two straight quarters — +121.4% in Q1 2026 and +90.6% in Q2 2026 — landing at 1.21% of portfolio, a real and growing commitment but still a modest single-digit-percent sizing, not a bet-the-fund position. Dodge & Cox added +164% in Q1 2026, but the resulting stake rounds to 0.0% of portfolio — a toehold position, immaterial in size. Read together, this is a couple of value shops nibbling on a statistically cheap, out-of-favor commodity name, not a high-conviction statement from a concentrated manager. It's mild corroboration that the multiple looks interesting to other value investors, not confirmation that the underlying economics or governance concerns have been resolved.

## Verdict
**Pass, conviction 6/10.** JBS is understandable and has genuine scale, but the moat is shallow (thin, price-taker margins), management trustworthiness is impaired by both leverage-dependent returns and a controlling family's documented governance history, predictability is low (commodity cycle dependent), and the valuation gap between reported earnings and actual cash generation erases the apparent cheapness once normalized. Superinvestor buying here is real but small-sized, corroborative at most. Pass, not because the business is hard to understand, but because the price does not compensate for the risks once owner earnings — not reported earnings — are the yardstick.
momentum_thesis: JBS is inflecting off a soft patch, not riding a clean trend: the 1-month tape is up 11.4%, but that's a bounce inside a -6.8% 3-month and -11.9% 6-month drawdown that's left the stock still 3.7% under its 200DMA, netting out to a flat +0.6% over 12 months. RSI14 at 60.8 confirms the bounce has legs without being overbought, so there's room to run before a momentum trader has to worry about exhaustion. Positioning reads as squeeze fuel rather than a bearish signal: 14.9% of float short with 6.9 days to cover is a heavy load for a defensive packaged-foods name, and the options market isn't hedging against it — a 0.053 put/call OI ratio is about as one-sided bullish as skew gets, meaning shorts are exposed with almost no put protection sitting behind them if the rally extends. That positioning lines up with the fundamental story: two value-oriented shops, Davis Advisors and Dodge & Cox, both added aggressively (+121% and +90% shares across Q1-Q2 2026 for Davis, +164% for Dodge & Cox in Q1) into a name trading at 12.2x trailing / 8.9x forward earnings — this isn't momentum chasing, it's value conviction arriving just as price technicals turn, which is the combination that tends to trap shorts. The catch is the balance sheet: 283% debt-to-equity against a 3.1% operating margin means the squeeze narrative has no fundamental cushion if the recovery stalls.
